planting.note: Plant a bare-root or containerized grafted tree in late winter while still dormant, in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Melrose begins bearing unusually young for a pecan, often within three to five years, and should be paired with a different-flowering-type cultivar such as Desirable or Cape Fear for good pollination.

directions: Melrose arose as a chance seedling discovered near Melrose Plantation in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, and was propagated for its unusually precocious habit of bearing a full crop years earlier than most named pecan cultivars. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil with plenty of room to spread, and provide a cultivar with an opposite pollen-shed pattern nearby to ensure full nut set. The medium-sized, well-filled nuts crack out easily and have good flavor, making Melrose a popular dooryard and home-orchard choice across the Gulf South even though it can show more scab susceptibility than newer disease-resistant releases in very humid seasons. Because it fruits so young, growers often use Melrose as a filler tree between longer-lived cultivars, removing it once the permanent trees begin bearing.

common_name: Frotscher Pecan (Frotscher's Egg Shell, Historic 1840s Louisiana Pecan)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late-winter dormancy in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Frotscher is among the oldest named pecan cultivars in cultivation and needs a long, warm growing season along with a cross-compatible pollinator to fill its large, thin-shelled nuts.

directions: Frotscher, sometimes recorded historically as Frotscher's Egg Shell, was selected and propagated near New Orleans in the 1840s, making it one of the earliest pecan cultivars ever given a name and grafted for orchard use, decades before most of today's commercial cultivars existed. It produces a notably large, thin-shelled nut with a high kernel percentage typical of the old Louisiana river-bottom selections that first drew commercial attention to pecans as an orchard crop. Give it deep, moist bottomland-type soil and full sun, and expect a large, spreading tree that needs a compatible pollinator for consistent nut set. Because of its age and rarity today, Frotscher is grown mostly by pecan-history enthusiasts and heritage orchards rather than commercial growers, who favor newer scab-resistant selections.

common_name: Money Maker Pecan (Historic Late-1800s Prolific Pecan)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Money Maker is a heavy annual producer of small-to-medium nuts and does best paired with a strong pollinator partner, since its heavy bearing can otherwise push it into an alternate-bearing cycle.

directions: Selected in the closing years of the 19th century, Money Maker earned its name from its reputation as a remarkably prolific bearer, often setting such a heavy crop that nut size and shell thickness suffer without regular thinning or fertilization. It was one of the mainstay commercial cultivars of the early Gulf South pecan industry before scab-resistant 20th-century releases largely replaced it in new plantings. The nuts are small to medium with a moderately thick shell, and the tree is more prone than modern cultivars to biennial bearing if not managed with attentive fertility and crop-thinning practices. Today it is grown mainly in older heritage orchards and by collectors interested in preserving historic pecan germplasm.

common_name: Burkett Pecan (Large-Nutted West Texas Commercial Pecan)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter while dormant in deep soil in full sun with reliable irrigation; Burkett is best suited to drier, low-humidity growing regions and needs a compatible pollinator, since it is notably more scab-prone than modern releases in humid climates.

directions: Discovered around 1912 as a chance seedling near San Saba, Texas, Burkett became one of the signature commercial pecan cultivars of the arid irrigated orchards of West Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. It produces a large, attractive, well-filled nut with excellent cracking quality that made it a favorite for retail and gift-pack sales under the Texas pecan label. Burkett performs best where humidity stays low, since it is notably more susceptible to pecan scab than modern disease-resistant cultivars and struggles in the humid Gulf South without an aggressive fungicide program. Give it full sun, deep soil, and reliable irrigation through nut fill, along with a compatible pollinator, for consistent large-nut production.

common_name: Gloria Grande Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Shade-and-Nut Pecan)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter dormancy in deep soil in full sun, allowing generous room for a large mature canopy; Gloria Grande's chief value is outstanding scab resistance, so it needs little fungicide input even in humid climates, but still benefits from a compatible pollinator cultivar.

directions: Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Gloria Grande was selected specifically for outstanding resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that devastates susceptible cultivars in the humid Southeast. It forms an unusually large, vigorous, long-lived tree, which has made it popular as a dual-purpose shade-and-nut planting for home landscapes and parks as well as orchards in high-scab-pressure regions. The nut itself is medium in size and only fair to good in kernel quality compared with top commercial dessert cultivars, so Gloria Grande is chosen more for reliability and low spray input than for exceptional eating quality. Plant it in full sun with deep soil and a compatible pollinator, and expect a tree that shades a wide area at maturity, so allow generous spacing from structures and other trees.

common_name: Villard Blanc Grape (Seyve-Villard 12-375, French-American Hybrid White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun on a well-drained site; Villard Blanc is a vigorous French-American hybrid bred for resistance to the fungal diseases that plague vinifera grapes in humid climates and performs best trained on a cordon or high-wire system with attentive canopy management.

directions: Villard Blanc, registered as Seyve-Villard 12-375, is one of the classic French-American hybrid wine grapes bred in the early 20th century by Bertille Seyve and Victor Villard to combine vinifera-quality fruit with the fungal-disease resistance of American parentage. It produces large clusters of greenish-white berries that ripen into a crisp, aromatic dry white wine and has historically been planted across the humid eastern and southern United States, where straight vinifera varieties struggle with black rot, downy mildew, and powdery mildew. Train vines on a cordon or high-wire trellis in full sun with good air movement, and prune hard each winter, since Villard Blanc is a vigorous grower that needs canopy management to ripen fruit well and avoid disease pressure in wet years. It carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance compared with purpose-bred Gulf Coast hybrids, so it performs best in the upper and middle South rather than the most humid Gulf Coast counties.
sources: Missouri State University Grape and Wine Program

common_name: Vidal Blanc Grape (Vidal 256, Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun on a well-drained site; Vidal Blanc is a heavy-cropping, cold-hardy French-American hybrid that ripens late in the season and often needs cluster thinning to keep wine quality high.

directions: Vidal Blanc, officially Vidal 256, is a French-American hybrid bred from Ugni Blanc and Seibel 4986 that has become one of the most widely planted white wine grapes in the eastern and southern United States for its combination of productivity, cold hardiness, and good fungal-disease tolerance. It produces heavy clusters of thick-skinned, golden berries late in the season, valued both for crisp dry table wines and for late-harvest or ice-wine-style dessert wines where hard freezes concentrate the sugars. Train it on a high-wire cordon or Geneva double-curtain system in full sun, and prune to manage its vigorous, fruitful growth, which can overcrop and require cluster thinning for best wine quality. Like most French-American hybrids, Vidal Blanc carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance, so southern extension programs generally recommend it for the upper and middle South rather than the most Pierce's-disease-prone Gulf Coast counties.
sources: Virginia Tech School of Plant and Environmental Sciences
Missouri State University Grape and Wine Institute

common_name: Lomanto Grape (Texas Hill Country Disease-Resistant Bunch Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun on well-drained, even thin or alkaline, soil; Lomanto's American parentage gives it good drought tolerance and Pierce's disease resistance once established on a sturdy trellis.

directions: Lomanto traces its parentage to the pioneering hybrid grape breeding work begun by T.V. Munson in Denison, Texas, which focused on combining native American Vitis species with European vinifera to create grapes tough enough for Texas heat, drought, alkaline soils, and Pierce's disease pressure. It bears clusters of small to medium dark red-black berries used mainly for juice, jelly, and home winemaking rather than fresh eating, with a tart, distinctly grapey flavor. Plant it on a sturdy trellis in full sun on well-drained soil, including thin, rocky, or alkaline sites where many other grapes struggle, since its American parentage gives it good drought tolerance and root vigor once established. It is a solid choice for home growers in the Texas Hill Country and greater Gulf South who want a low-input bunch grape without the spray program vinifera varieties demand.
sources: Texas Wine and Grape Growers Association
